name: Suriname
sources: GDP $0.577bn and 409,000 people in 1990 (World Bank NY.GDP.MKTP.CD and SP.POP.TOTL, via countryeconomy.com; real growth -1.5%).

THE GDP FIGURE IS THE UNRELIABLE ONE IN THIS FILE AND THE SIZE OF THE PROBLEM IS VISIBLE IN THE SERIES ITSELF. The same source prints Surinamese output per head at $5,330 in 1989 and $1,412 in 1990 - a 73.5% fall in dollars in a year the real economy shrank 1.5%. Nothing happened to Suriname in 1990 that destroyed three quarters of its economy. What happened is the exchange rate: the guilder was pegged at 1.785 SRG to the dollar and had been since 1940, the parallel rate was somewhere between 10 and 30, and the conversion factor the series applies changes between the two years. The honest statement is that Surinamese dollar GDP in 1990 is anywhere between $0.5bn and $2bn depending entirely on which rate is used, that this is exactly the failure the brief for this roster names - a command-adjacent economy converted at an official rate - and that $0.577bn is entered because it is what the series the rest of the roster sits on says. Every ratio below that has GDP in its denominator inherits the uncertainty.

Inflation 21.8% for 1990 (7.3% in 1988, 0.8% in 1989, 10.5% in 1991). The low prints of the late 1980s are price control and a fixed peg, not price stability; the collapse comes later and is large - the series reaches 368% in 1994 - and none of that is written into this file. interest_rate 0.15 against it leaves the real rate about 6 points below neutral. UNVERIFIED: Surinamese rates in 1990 were administratively set inside an exchange-control regime and no World Bank lending series covers the year, so 0.15 is placed rather than transcribed and is the weakest number here after the GDP.

Revenue 19.6% of GDP, arrived at from government expenditure of 22.67% of GDP and a deficit of 3.04% of GDP for 1990 (countryeconomy.com). Government debt $385m, 72.88% of GDP, entered as 0.73. Both ratios carry the exchange-rate caveat above.

Gross capital formation entered as 10% public and 8% private, an apportionment and not two transcriptions - the least defensible pair of numbers in the file. Dutch development aid under the 1975 independence treaty had been suspended since the December murders of 1982 and was not restored until 1991, which removed the main source of Surinamese public investment for the whole of the period this start state describes.

Oil 0.004 mbd: Staatsolie produced 3,900 barrels a day in 1990 from the Tambaredjo field in Saramacca (EIA series via IndexMundi; 3,000 in 1988, 4,000 in 1989, 3,500 in 1991). Genuinely tiny and genuinely there. The economy that mattered was bauxite and alumina - Suralco and Billiton - which this schema has no field for.

Military 3.0% of GDP and strength 0.5, for a Nationaal Leger of roughly 2,000 men. UNVERIFIED: SIPRI carries no series for Suriname and no budget figure was retrieved, so the 3.0% is placed from the size of the force and the fact that it was fighting a civil war, and it should be treated as an order-of-magnitude statement rather than a transcription. What is not uncertain is the force's political weight, which is out of all proportion to the number: Desi Bouterse had led the sergeants' coup of 25 February 1980, ruled directly until 1987, and remained army commander over the civilian government in January 1990.

Stability 33 - the lowest in this region's roster - and separatism 0.16. Suriname in January 1990 is a state at war with itself. The Binnenlandse Oorlog had run since July 1986: Ronnie Brunswijk's Jungle Commando, drawn from the Ndyuka Maroons of the east, held much of the interior against the army, which answered with the Moiwana massacre of 29 November 1986 and drove some 10,000 refugees into French Guiana. The Kwinti and Tucayana Amazonas were fighting too, on their own account. That is a territorial insurgency by a distinct people over a defined region, which is what separatism means here, and 0.16 places it above Bolivia's 0.10 indigenous and regional strain and below an actual partition.

authoritarianism 0.45 for a country with a real election and no real civilian control. Ramsewak Shankar was elected president by the National Assembly in January 1988 after a genuine vote on 25 November 1987 in which the opposition Front took 85.5% - and Bouterse kept the army, kept a constitutional role written for him, and removed the government by telephone on 24 December 1990. None of that outcome is encoded: the polity block in government.rs carries the 1987 shares, the army as a pillar, and an election due at the end of the constitutional term.
